You're doing the right thing by learning about Bitcoin now rather than later.

The best way to get Bitcoins is to buy to sell something for them. Cutting banks out of the transaction is always a wise move, so use cash, before it is banned in a few years. Banks want to ban cash so they can monitor every transaction you make. I would look at getting a Case Hardware Wallet or a Trezor, if Case isn't available.

There are many ways to purchase bitcoin, your options depend on where you are. In the US and Europe you can connect your bank account to Coinbase and convert some of your bank balance into bitcoin-cash near instantly. In that case you're 'purchasing' bitcoin directly from Coinbase. There are many bitcoin currency exchanges you can choose from as well - basically Forex exchanges that specialize in bitcoin. Bitstamp, Bitfinex, OKCoin, BTC-e, etc. They have a variety of ways to open and fund an account (wire transfer for instance.) Localbitcoins.com is a bit different - it allows individuals to buy and sell from each other, either face-to-face cash, bank transfers, paypal, etc.. You could also use meetup.com and find a bitcoin meetup where you could purchase some directly face-to-face.

If you use an exchange like Coinbase or Bitstamp then yes, the bank knows (and the government if they asked) that you've transferred money to a Bitcoin exchange. The only way buying bitcoin can be close to anonymous is if you use anonymous money to start with ($20 bills to a stranger in an alley. ;)

After that it gets complicated. The blockchain is a record of every transaction, ever. (that's the brilliant invention that makes the whole system work.) 100 yrs in the future someone could trace back a transaction from the sale receipt with your shipping address to the bank account with your name on it - unless you essentially launder the bitcoin in the middle. That's actually fairly easy. Bitcoin can absolutely be used anonymously if you want to. (It's also easy to screw it up and accidentally de-anonymize your past spending.)

There are different ways to create a bitcoin wallet. I don't recommend running bitcoin core on your own machine until you know a 'bit' more (pun). Using an online wallet service like Coinbase is pretty much the same as having a bank or paypal account, except that you own bitcoin instead of inflatable bank-money. If you want to "be your own" bank - to have absolute control of your own money - then you want to use the Bitcoin network itself. As long as you have the signing key that controls a particular address those coins can sit there for years. You can spend them when ever you want to. For secure savings many people make a paper wallet - essentially you print out the secret key to an address you've sent some coins to and then you delete any copy of that key from your computer. (Hacker's can't 'hack' a piece of paper you've hidden under a floorboard.)

I buy (and sell) my bitcoin with Coinbase. I don't, however, use my wallet there to store or spend them. I transfer them to a wallet I control (using various ways to break the connection to their Coinbase origin before I spend them on something I don't want connected to my identity - such as wikileaks donations.)

Personally, for a wallet YOU control, I recommend blockchain.info The way their service works is as an in-browser javascript app. The addresses and signing keys for your wallet are created in your browser and encrypted by your passphrase before being saved on blockchain.info's servers for convenience. There are several additional safeguards to keep from ever losing access to your wallet even if the service disappeared in the future, but the critical part is that they do not have access to your money. They have a mobile app that makes it trivial to actually USE your bitcoin as well. They also have a TOR hidden service front end, so you can create completely anonymous wallets. As a plus, they have an option to use the CoinJoin algorithm as a Shared Send, which is the safest way to 'launder' bitcoin, although it doesn't necessarily 'clean' them as well as using a mixing service.

But gold has no more "intrinsic value" than bitcoin, contrary to what opponents of bitcoin argue. If society collapses, a few grams of a shiny, soft and electrically conducting metal has no real value, as opposed to clean water, canned food and a pair of shoes. This "value" is not easily expressed in $, any more than the intrinsic value of the Internet Protocol, but I argue it's real. The term "wallet" basically refers to a public key (or address, think like email address, its a string of numbers and letters) and a private key (the thing you don't share with anyone, and it looks like a very long string of numbers and letters).

You can make brand new perfectly unique bitcoin addresses (or wallets) all day every day for free, and you never need to do anything to keep that address (besides hold onto the public/private key pairs). If u use a wallet provider (like coinbase, etc) then you may or may not be subjected to fees by the provider... but if you learn get what your'e doing u wont' necessarily need providers all the time.

There are lots of different types of "wallets" and they can all be used for different purposes and levels of security. A simple wallet is a "paper wallet." Basically, its just a public/private key pair that's printed on paper. You scan the public key to recieve money, and your private key to send. It's best used as a form of storage, and not best if you use the same address to send more than once.

Another form of wallet is a hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet. This uses a "seed" (think super secret password code) to create many public/private key pairs. As long as you have the seed you can recreate all the public/private keys. Mycelium wallet does this.

While the three do have similar qualities (including the above traits you've mentioned), there are many differences.

Firstly, language:

In Singapore, the main language used is English, but most are bilingual, speaking Mandarin, Malay, Tamil, etc. in addition to speaking English.

In Hong Kong, the main language used is Cantonese. However the community there (in the city areas) are quite international, so there are quite a number of English speakers there.

In Taiwan, the main language is Mandarin, and a dialect called Taiwanese, or Hokkien (this is also used quite widely amongst the Chinese population in Singapore, though there are differences)

While written Chinese is used in all three countries, Singapore uses simplified characters (same as China), while Hong Kong and Taiwan uses traditional characters. The word for "close" in mandarin: 闭 (Simplified) & 閉 (Traditional). Cantonese is written using chinese characters, but different words and characters are used from Mandarin. "Shut up" in mandarin 閉嘴/閉嘴, and "shut up" in Cantonese 冇嘈. Also, Mandarin uses for phonetic tones while in Cantonese there are nine. Also different Mandarin words are used in Singapore and Taiwan for certain things. "Market" is referred to as 市场 in Taiwan but 把沙 in Singapore (sounding instead like the Malay word for market - pasar).

Regarding English, Singaporeans use a special subset of it called Singlish.

I can elaborate more on the language differences if anyone is interested.

Singapore is a very small place, so it is packed to the brim with skyscrapers and other buildings. There is still a lot of greenery (planted) though. It's also a young country and many things are still new. Hong Kong Island in Hong Kong is like an even more compressed version of Singapore, but moving upwards into Kowloon and the New Territories there are more rural and untouched places. There are also many places rich in history and culture. Taipei City is comparable to these two places, although there is more space between things, and it never gets as crowded. Lots of scooters compared to cars on the roads. The rest of Taiwan is less city-like. Many nature-y places.

Perhaps I can elaborate more on more specific questions as yours is pretty broad, but I hope you can see that these places are far from identical!

"seafood" - it did not get much fresher than picking your meal out of the aquarium tanks along to store fronts on the water. Is that an island thing or a (local) tourist thing? I have not seen that in the big cities.

It's more of an island thing. Taipei has a super fresh market where there are 'standing' restaurants. They prepare the food right there and then with the fresh ingredients and you stand at a counter and eat. You should check it out if you're fond of seafood and happen to be in Taiwan.
I'd love to go to Taipei but I don't see it happening in my business travels. I did have a nice view of it flying over from HK to Tokyo.

• Which of these countries would you most like to live in long-term?

  • What are the downsides of each country (I know that Hong Kong is really crowded, for example)?

  • Did you go to an international school? How did you deal with the disruptions in your life by moving around?

It is really hard to decide because I do have an attachment to each. I feel like my course of study could even lead me to a job outside the three. My nationality is still Singaporean, so I do have benefits staying in Singapore. Cons would be no seasons, not many things to do, and I would have to return to the military each year for a period of time. Hong Kong I really like, but I feel that I'm biased to it because that was when I spent my middle years and made most of my BFFs. But the place has a nice mix of AC during summer and outdoor hiking/cycling trails during winter. Oh, also my girlfriend is studying there now and might end up working there. So there's that. I would need to brush up on my Cantonese first though. Taiwan is where my family is based at now, but that might change again in the future. Running in Taiwan is something I really enjoyed because it's less crowded, many hills, and the scenery is gorgeous. The Japanese food (my favourite) also easily wins out against Singapore's and Hong Kong's.

Tldr; I really don't know, it's too hard to choose and I might be elsewhere even.

As for the downsides of each place.. Hong Kong people have a rep for being unfriendly but I don't think that holds as true anymore. Perhaps it is only the people visiting from China, that can be found in many of the tourist attractions in Taiwan as well. I feel like the crowd is more pleasant to be in though. People keep to themselves though they might talk loudly. Train etiquette is observed. Whereas in Singapore there is a lot of staring going on on trains and some people don't like queuing properly. Though I feel there are many different types of people I both places so it's hard to generalize. Hong Kong air is definitely worse that the other two, but there are areas where it's very fresh and clean. There's some haze sometimes from Indonesia in Singapore, but the air is clean. It does get very humid though. Out of the three Taiwan is the only one that gets earthquakes. Things are very expensive in Singapore and Hong Kong.

I did go to an international school in both Hong Kong (pre IB program, more European styled), and Taiwan (American school). I am a very sentimental person that really values friendship so moving each time was very hard. However I did make many friends in HK because I guess that was when you grow up and become independent together with a group of people. Leaving HK was probably the hardest thing I had to do in my life and I was pretty devastated for a long period. I did not make many friends in Taiwan, perhaps due to this, or because it was just a different crowd. However because it was an American school there was a big focus on sports, so I did find camaraderie in the Cross Country and Track teams, where there was training 5-6 times a week. I also really enjoyed the IB, and spent a lot of time on my studies (as I didn't have much of a social life outside of sports). I guess this was how I eventually dealt with moving to Taiwan, by focusing on other things like sports and academics. I also did go back to HK during Christmases to visit my old friends and kept in touch with most of them.
